834.title: Call me bitter (Ruth 1:1–21)
834.hook: Naomi loses husband and sons in Moab and asks to be called Mara, bitter
834.carry: stay beside them, let their words stand
834.tomorrow: Thy people shall be my people (Ruth 1:16–17)
834.howItsDone: The book of Ruth is read in synagogue on Shavuot, and Jews count it among the short scrolls of the Writings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Writings opened: songs, wisdom and stories in human voices. Your line was they praise, they doubt, they complain. What did you write down by hand? Today, the first story on the Talmud's list, and a woman who wants a new name. Day eight hundred thirty-four.

Two women walk into Bethlehem, dusty from the road, and the whole town comes out to look. In the King James, "all the city was moved about them, and they said, Is this Naomi?" Is this her? She left with a husband and two sons. She's come back with none of them, and the woman beside her is a foreigner from Moab. The neighbors aren't cruel. They're just shocked. They knew her face, and they can barely match it to the one in front of them. And Naomi answers the question in a way nobody expects. She tells them to stop using her name.
screen: `TWO WOMEN WALK INTO BETHLEHEM.` → `IS THIS NAOMI?` → `STOP USING MY NAME.`

segments.voice: Go back to how the book begins: "in the days when the judges ruled," a famine in the land. A man of Bethlehem, Elimelech, takes his wife Naomi and their two sons across to the fields of Moab to survive. There Elimelech dies. The sons marry Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth. Then both sons die. The King James puts it in one bare line: "the woman was left of her two sons and her husband." Left. That's the word for her. When she hears there's bread again at home, she sets out, and on the road she begs her daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers. Orpah, weeping, goes. Ruth won't. That moment is tomorrow's. Today belongs to Naomi at the city gate. "Call me not Naomi, call me Mara: for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me." Mara means bitter. Then: "I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me home again empty." Notice three things. First, she says it out loud, in public, and she says it about God. She doesn't pretend to be fine for the neighbors. Second, the book doesn't correct her. No one tells her to look on the bright side. Her words are kept, exactly as she said them, in Scripture. Third, and this is the quiet ache of the chapter: when Naomi says empty, Ruth is standing right next to her. The one person who stayed. Grief that deep can't see it yet, and the story doesn't rush her. It only adds, at the end of the chapter, that they arrived at the beginning of barley harvest.
screen: `A FAMINE, MOAB, AND THREE GRAVES.` · `THE WOMAN WAS LEFT.` · then, large: `CALL ME NOT NAOMI, CALL ME MARA.` · then: `SHE SAYS EMPTY, AND RUTH IS THERE.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit with someone who lost much. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is carrying a heavy loss: a death, a divorce, a home, a job, a body that doesn't work the way it did. Don't fix it. Don't look for the bright side for them. Just let them be as bitter as they are, the way the book lets Naomi be. In your mind, stand beside them at the gate, saying nothing, staying. If you pray, you can hold them before God without words. If you can, decide on one small way to sit with them this week, in person or in a message. The bell holds the time.
Mara. Hebrew for bitter, the name Naomi asks to be called, home from Moab with her husband and sons buried, and the book lets her say it. Today's word.
Your line: stay beside them, let their words stand. Today, when someone tells you how hard it is, don't correct them. Day eight hundred thirty-four.

835.title: Thy people shall be my people (Ruth 1:16–17)
835.word: Thy people shall be my people
835.hook: Ruth clings to Naomi: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God"
835.howItsDone: Jews read Ruth's vow in the book of Ruth on Shavuot, and Jewish tradition looks to Ruth as the example of someone who joins the Jewish people by choice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naomi at the gate of Bethlehem asked to be called Mara. Your line was stay beside them, let their words stand. Whose hard words did you let stand? Today, we step back onto the road, before the gate, to hear what Ruth said. Day eight hundred thirty-five.
screen: `STAY BESIDE THEM, LET THEIR WORDS STAND.`

segments.voice: On the road out of Moab, Naomi keeps sending her daughters-in-law home, and her argument is practical, almost brutal. I'm too old to have a husband. Even if I had sons tonight, would you wait for them to grow up? Go back. Orpah weeps, kisses her, and turns for home, and the book never blames her. Ruth doesn't move. So Naomi points down the road at the figure getting smaller. In the King James: "Behold, thy sister in law is gone back unto her people, and unto her gods: return thou after thy sister in law." It's the last door Naomi can open for her. And Ruth closes it.
screen: `GO BACK, I HAVE NOTHING TO GIVE.` → `ORPAH TURNS FOR HOME.` → `RETURN THOU AFTER THY SISTER.`

segments.voice: Ruth's answer holds the line in today's title: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." Today, listen to how it ends. "Where thou diest, will I die, and there will I be buried: the LORD do so to me, and more also, if ought but death part thee and me." Three things are packed in there. First, she goes past a lifetime. Not just I'll come with you, but I'll be buried where you're buried. Not even her bones are going back to Moab. Second, she seals it with an oath, and she swears by the LORD, the name of Naomi's God. A woman of Moab, on a road out of Moab, binds herself in the name she's choosing. Third, and this is easy to miss, look at what Naomi does. "When she saw that she was stedfastly minded to go with her, then she left speaking unto her." That's all. No embrace in the text. No thank you. Naomi just stops arguing, and they walk on, and the next thing she says out loud, at the gate, is that she came home empty. Ruth's loyalty isn't thanked on the spot. It doesn't need to be. The rabbis heard even more in these lines. In the Talmud, in tractate Yevamot, they imagine a whole conversation hidden in the speech: Naomi naming, one by one, what this life will ask of her, and each of Ruth's phrases answering, I accept. And some readers find one word under all of it, a word Ruth never says but lives out: chesed, loyal kindness that keeps going after it's been told to stop.

segments.voice: Today, the practice is to stay loyal to someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is hard to stay with right now. Not someone who harms you; someone who is grieving, prickly, distant, or just not saying thank you. A parent, a friend, a sibling, a neighbor. Walk beside them in your mind, on a long road, with nothing being said. Ask what staying would look like this week: a call you keep making, a visit, a seat saved, a message that asks for nothing back. Choose one. If you pray, you can say their name to God as you walk. The bell holds the time.

836.title: Some handfuls (Ruth 2)
836.hook: Boaz tells his workers to "let fall also some of the handfuls" for her
836.howItsDone: Jewish teaching on giving, rooted in the laws of leaving gleanings and the corners of the field, prizes gifts that protect the dignity of the one who receives, and the book of Ruth is read in synagogue on Shavuot.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth's vow on the road: thy people shall be my people, and Naomi's silence. Your line was thy people, my people. Where did you keep showing up without thanks? Today, the two women are home, and they need to eat. Day eight hundred thirty-six.

The King James has a lovely way of saying it just happened: "her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz." Ruth goes out to glean, to pick up the stalks the reapers drop, which the Torah leaves for the poor and the stranger. She wanders into one field among many. And the owner, it so happens, walks out from Bethlehem right then, and the first thing out of his mouth is a greeting to his workers: "The LORD be with you." And they call back: "The LORD bless thee." A boss and his reapers, blessing each other in the barley. Then he notices the stranger.
screen: `HER HAP WAS TO LIGHT ON THIS FIELD.` → `THE LORD BE WITH YOU.` → `HE NOTICES THE STRANGER.`

segments.voice: Boaz asks who she is, and hears: the Moabite girl who came back with Naomi. So he tells her: stay in my field, drink from the water my young men draw, I've told them not to touch you. Ruth falls on her face. "Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I am a stranger?" His answer: I've heard everything you did for your mother-in-law, how you left your father and mother and the land you were born in. And he blesses her by the God "under whose wings thou art come to trust." At mealtime he hands her roasted grain, and she eats until she's full and has some left over, which she saves for Naomi. Now the line in today's title. When Ruth gets up to glean again, Boaz quietly gives his reapers an order: "let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her, and leave them, that she may glean them, and rebuke her not." Listen to how he does it. He doesn't hand her a sack of grain in front of everyone. He has the extra dropped on purpose, where she'll find it, so it looks like ordinary gleaning. She gets to gather it with her own hands. And rebuke her not: nobody stands over her, nobody makes her feel watched. The gift is real, and her dignity stays whole. That evening she carries home so much barley that Naomi asks where she worked. Ruth says the name: Boaz. And the woman who came home empty, who asked to be called bitter, says: "Blessed be he of the LORD, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead." Mara is blessing someone again.
screen: `WHY HAVE I FOUND GRACE, A STRANGER?` · `UNDER WHOSE WINGS THOU ART COME TO TRUST.` · then, large: `LET FALL SOME OF THE HANDFULS OF PURPOSE.` · then: `REBUKE HER NOT: DIGNITY KEPT.` · then: `THE EMPTY ONE BLESSES AGAIN.`

segments.voice: This practice comes straight from the field: leave something extra for someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a person who could use a little more than they have, but who would hate to be handed charity. A coworker stretched thin. A neighbor living alone. A student, a parent, a friend between jobs. Now think like Boaz. How could you let a handful fall where they'll find it? Food that happens to be left over. A bigger tip than usual. A ride offered as if it's on your way. Choose one, and choose the quiet way to do it. If you pray, you can hold them under the wings Boaz spoke of. The bell holds the time.
Some handfuls. The grain Boaz has dropped on purpose for Ruth to glean, so the gift comes without shame. Today's word.

837.title: From outsider to ancestor (Ruth 4)
837.hook: the Moabite woman becomes the great-grandmother of King David
837.tomorrow: A man in the land of Uz
837.howItsDone: Jewish communities read the book of Ruth on the festival of Shavuot, and Ruth is remembered in Jewish tradition as a woman who chose to join the Jewish people and as an ancestor of King David.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Boaz told his workers to drop a little extra grain where Ruth was gleaning. Your line was let fall some handfuls. What did you leave behind for someone else to find? Today, the last chapter of Ruth. Day eight hundred thirty-seven.

The book of Ruth ends with a list of names. But before the list, there's a morning at the city gate. Boaz goes up and sits down there, the place where a town did its business. A relative of Naomi's walks by, a nearer kinsman than Boaz, and Boaz calls him over. He gathers elders of the city as witnesses. Then he lays it out: Naomi is selling a piece of land, and the nearer kinsman has the first right to buy it back. Sure, the man says, I'll redeem it. Then Boaz adds the rest. The land comes with Ruth, the Moabite widow, and with keeping her late husband's name alive. The man backs out. He pulls off his shoe and hands it over, the old way of sealing a deal, and the field and the future pass to Boaz.
screen: `A MORNING AT THE CITY GATE.` → `THE NEARER KINSMAN BACKS OUT.` → `A SHOE SEALS THE DEAL.`

segments.voice: Notice what the book keeps calling her, right up to the end. Not Ruth the wife of Boaz. Ruth the Moabitess. Back in chapter two she called herself a foreigner, and the story never pretends otherwise. She marries Boaz, and a son is born. And then the camera swings away from the parents to Naomi. Naomi, who came home empty and asked to be called bitter. The women of Bethlehem gather around her and praise Ruth to her face. In the King James words, they call her "thy daughter in law, which loveth thee, which is better to thee than seven sons." Seven sons, said to a woman who buried two. Naomi takes the baby and lays him in her lap and cares for him. Then the neighbors give him a name, and here's the line the whole book has been walking toward: "There is a son born to Naomi; and they called his name Obed: he is the father of Jesse, the father of David." David. His great-grandmother came from Moab, a people the Torah elsewhere keeps out of the assembly. The rabbis noticed that tension. The Talmud records a reading that the old rule names Moabite men, not Moabite women, which left a door open for Ruth. The book itself just ends with the family line, generation by generation, and the last name on it is David. Tradition reads this book on Shavuot, the festival of receiving the Torah, and some readers hear why: Ruth chose to come in. A story that began with a famine and three graves ends with a cradle and a king. The outsider was never made to stop being an outsider. She became an ancestor anyway.
screen: `STILL CALLED RUTH THE MOABITESS.` · `BETTER THAN SEVEN SONS.` · `A SON BORN TO NAOMI.` · then, large: `THE FATHER OF JESSE, THE FATHER OF DAVID.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor an outsider in your story. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who came into your family or your life from somewhere else. A stepparent. An in-law. A grandparent who arrived in a new country with a suitcase. A neighbor who became family. Hold their face for a moment. Then ask: what came into my life through them? A recipe, a word, a way of holding a baby, a reason I'm here at all. Let the breath carry their name in and out. If you pray, you can name them before God with thanks. The bell holds the time.
From outsider to ancestor. Ruth the Moabitess, a foreigner gleaning in Bethlehem, becomes the great-grandmother of King David. Today's word.

838.title: A man in the land of Uz (Job 1:1–12)
838.word: A man in the land of Uz
838.hook: a blameless man, and the adversary's question: does he serve for nothing?
838.howItsDone: Job is one of the books of the Writings, the third part of the Tanakh. Jews study it as a book of wisdom and argument about suffering, and traditional study includes the rabbis' debate over whether Job was a real man or a parable.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ruth the Moabitess became the great-grandmother of King David. Your line was from outsider to ancestor. Whose name did you say out loud? Today, a new book in the Writings: Job. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

"There was a man in the land of Uz, whose name was Job." That's how it opens, like a story told at bedtime. No king's name, no year, no map. The book never says where Uz is. The man is good, the text says, perfect and upright, one who feared God and turned away from evil. He has sons and daughters, flocks and herds, a full house. His children throw feasts, taking turns at each other's homes, and after every round Job gets up early and offers sacrifices for them, just in case one of them sinned and cursed God in their heart. A careful father. A man with nothing to hide. And then the scene changes, and we're not in Uz anymore.
screen: `A MAN IN THE LAND OF UZ.` → `PERFECT AND UPRIGHT.` → `UP EARLY FOR HIS CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: We're in heaven, at a gathering before God, and one of those who comes is called, in Hebrew, ha-satan. The word has "the" in front of it: the adversary, the accuser. Here he isn't a ruler of his own kingdom. He shows up with the others and answers to God. God speaks first: "Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth?" And the adversary asks the question the whole book will live inside: "Doth Job fear God for nought?" For nothing. Look at the fence you've put around him, he says. His house, his work, his flocks. Take it away, and he'll curse you to your face. And God allows it: everything Job has is in your hand, but don't touch the man himself. Then the adversary goes out, and Job knows none of this. That's the strange gift of this book. We, the readers, know why it's happening. Job never does. Some readers hear the question turned on themselves. Is goodness a deal? Am I kind because it works, honest because it pays, faithful because life has gone well? Or is there something underneath that would still be there if the rewards stopped? The rabbis didn't agree on who Job was. In the Talmud, one teacher says Job never lived at all, that the book is a parable, and others argue for different ages and places. Either way, the question lands on the reader. Uz could be anywhere. The man could be anyone.
screen: `HA-SATAN: THE ADVERSARY.` · `DOTH JOB FEAR GOD FOR NOUGHT?` · `WE KNOW WHY. JOB NEVER DOES.` · `A REAL MAN, OR A PARABLE?`

segments.voice: Today, sit with one unfair question. Settle, and breathe. Let the adversary's question come close, turned gently toward your own life. Pick one good thing you do: calling your mother, showing up to work honest, giving, praying, being patient with a kid. Then ask it quietly: would I still do this if nothing came back? Don't answer. Don't defend yourself. Don't decide you're a fraud or a saint. Just let the question sit in the room with you, the way it sits at the start of this book, unanswered. Breathe in, and hold it. Breathe out, and let it stay. If you pray, you can bring the question to God as it is. The bell holds the time.
A man in the land of Uz. Job, a good man in a place no one can find on a map, and the question asked about him in heaven. Today's word.

segments.voice: Your line: is it for nothing. Today, do one good thing nobody will see or thank you for, and notice how it feels to do it for nothing. Day eight hundred thirty-eight.

839.title: Gave and taken (Job 1:20–22)
839.hook: "the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away"
839.howItsDone: Jewish mourners tear a garment, called keriah, when they learn of a close relative's death, and Job's words, the LORD gave and the LORD has taken away, are part of the traditional Jewish burial service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the adversary asked God about Job: does he serve for nothing? Your line was is it for nothing. Did you do one good thing nobody saw? Today, the question gets its first answer. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

A messenger runs up to Job. Raiders came, he says, and took the oxen and the donkeys, and killed the servants, "and I only am escaped alone to tell thee." While he's still speaking, a second runs in: fire fell from the sky and burned up the sheep. While he's still speaking, a third: raiders took the camels. While he's still speaking, a fourth. Your sons and daughters were eating together in their oldest brother's house, and a great wind came from the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell on them. They're dead. The text gives us no pause between the messengers. That's the point. It all lands at once.
screen: `WHILE HE WAS YET SPEAKING.` → `ONE MESSENGER, THEN ANOTHER.` → `THE HOUSE FALLS.`

segments.voice: Now watch what Job does, in order, because the order matters. "Then Job arose, and rent his mantle, and shaved his head, and fell down upon the ground, and worshipped." He tears his robe. He shaves his head. He falls to the ground. Grief comes first, and it's physical, and the book doesn't hurry him past it. Jewish mourners still tear a garment at a death; the tearing is called keriah. Only then, from the ground, Job speaks: "Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD." Two things in one breath. Everything I had was given; none of it was mine to keep. And still, from the floor, a blessing. Not a blessing instead of grief. A blessing in the middle of it, with the robe already torn. The narrator adds one line: "In all this Job sinned not, nor charged God foolishly." The adversary said Job would curse God to his face. He doesn't. Tradition put Job's words into the Jewish burial service, so mourners say this line at the graveside. Some find it a comfort. Some find it almost impossible to say. Both are honest, and the book of Job has room for both: this isn't Job's last word. He'll have much more to say, and not all of it gentle. But today, this is where he stands, or rather kneels.
screen: `HE TEARS HIS ROBE AND FALLS.` · `NAKED CAME I, NAKED SHALL I RETURN.` · then, large: `THE LORD GAVE, AND THE LORD HATH TAKEN AWAY.` · then: `NOT HIS LAST WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit quietly with a loss. Settle, and breathe. Let one loss come to mind. It might be a person. It might be a home, a job, a friendship, a version of your life you thought you'd have. There's nothing to solve here, and no moral to find. Just let it sit beside you, the way Job sat on the ground. Breathe in, and notice it was given. Breathe out, and notice it was taken. You don't have to bless anything. If you pray, and if the words fit today, you can say Job's line. If they don't fit, the silence is enough. The bell holds the time.
Gave and taken. Job, on the ground in a torn robe, says what was given was never his to keep, and blesses anyway. Today's word.
Your line: gave and taken. Today, touch one thing you love, a photo, a cup, a hand, and remember that it was given. Day eight hundred thirty-nine.

840.title: Seven silent days (Job 2:11–13)
840.hook: Job's friends sit with him seven days without a word, the best thing they do
840.howItsDone: During shiva, the week of mourning, Jewish mourners stay at home and visitors come to comfort them; by tradition visitors wait for the mourner to speak first, a custom the Talmud ties to Job's friends.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Job tore his robe and said, the LORD gave and the LORD hath taken away. Your line was gave and taken. This week ran from Naomi's bitterness, through Ruth's promise and the handfuls left in the field, to King David's family line, and into the land of Uz. It ends in silence. Day eight hundred forty.

It gets worse. In chapter two the adversary comes back, and this time Job's own body is struck, with sore boils from the sole of his foot to the top of his head. He sits down among the ashes and scrapes his skin with a broken piece of pottery. His wife tells him to curse God and die. He answers her: "shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?" Somewhere far off, three friends hear the news: Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar. They arrange to meet, and they travel to Job together, to mourn with him and comfort him.
screen: `BOILS, ASHES, A BROKEN POT.` → `SHALL WE NOT RECEIVE EVIL?` → `THREE FRIENDS SET OUT.`

segments.voice: From a distance, they don't recognize him. That's the first thing the text says when they arrive. Then they weep out loud. They tear their robes. They throw dust into the air, so it falls on their heads. And then comes the line this day is named for: "So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great." They sat down with him. On the ground, in the ashes, at his level. Not in chairs above him. And none of them spoke. The reason is right there in the verse: they saw. They looked at their friend and understood that this grief was bigger than anything they could say. Some readers call this the best thing the friends do in the whole book. Hold on to that, because in the coming days they'll start talking. The rabbis learned something practical from this scene. The Talmud teaches that people who come to comfort a mourner shouldn't speak until the mourner speaks first, and it draws that rule from Job: his friends waited, and Job opened his mouth. Jewish mourning still has a week of sitting, called shiva, when the family stays home and visitors come to them. The custom is to come in, sit down, and let the mourner lead. It's a hard skill. When someone is hurting, the urge to fill the air is strong: an explanation, a story, a bright side. The friends, for seven days, resisted it. They brought only themselves.
screen: `THEY DIDN'T RECOGNIZE HIM.` · `THEY SAT DOWN WITH HIM.` · then, large: `NONE SPAKE A WORD UNTO HIM.` · then: `WAIT FOR THE MOURNER TO SPEAK.`

segments.voice: For one sit, do what the friends did, and sit silently with someone. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who is carrying something heavy right now. Picture sitting beside them, on the floor if you like, close enough to touch shoulders. Now notice the words that rise up to fix it. Let each one come, and let it go unsaid. Stay. Just stay. If you pray, you can hold them before God without words. And if there's someone near you right now, a partner, a parent, a friend, you might sit with them for a minute later today, with nothing to say. The bell holds the time.
Shiva. The seven days Job's friends sat on the ground with him, saying nothing, because they saw how great his grief was. Today's word.
Your line: they said nothing. Today, when someone tells you something hard, let a few seconds of silence go by before you answer. Day eight hundred forty.
